body:
Santorini is one of those places where renting a car seems like the obvious answer.

Until wine enters the plan.

The island’s wineries are scattered between villages such as Pyrgos, Megalochori, Exo Gonia, Vothonas and Oia.

That is part of the charm.

It is also the practical problem.

If you want to taste Assyrtiko, Nychteri and Vinsanto properly, somebody has to think about transport.

And that person should probably not be the one doing the tasting.

## Why a wine tour makes more sense here than on many islands

Santorini’s wineries are not concentrated in one walkable district.

Some sit above the caldera.

Others are hidden in inland villages.

Some occupy old cave-like cellars cut into volcanic ground.

Visit Greece specifically highlights areas such as Megalochori, Pyrgos, Exo Gonia, Vothonas and Oia as part of the island’s wine landscape.

That means a self-guided tasting day usually involves planning several separate journeys.

A dedicated wine tour removes most of that friction.

You are collected, driven between wineries, given time to taste, and returned afterward.

That is not glamorous.

It is simply sensible.

## Option 1: A small-group winery tour

This is the easiest choice for most visitors.

A typical small-group tour visits several wineries over three to four hours and includes transport plus tastings.

One current Viator itinerary, for example, combines:

- Canava Roussos
- the Koutsogiannopoulos Wine Museum
- Venetsanos Winery

The attraction here is variety.

You get a traditional winery, a wine museum and a caldera-side winery in a single outing.

For someone visiting Santorini for the first time, that is a useful introduction to the island’s wine culture without spending the entire day organising taxis or parking.

**Best for:** first-time visitors, couples and anyone who wants a simple half-day experience.

## Option 2: Wine plus sunset

Santorini does sunsets rather aggressively.

People plan entire evenings around them.

So combining wine and sunset is one of the few tourist clichés that actually makes practical sense.

Some island tours include a winery stop before continuing toward the evening sunset.

Venetsanos is especially well positioned for this because the winery sits above the caldera near Megalochori.

Visit Greece even recommends enjoying Vinsanto from the cooperative winery above Pyrgos while looking across the caldera.

The important distinction is this:

A general sunset tour with one tasting stop is not the same thing as a proper wine tour.

Choose this option if the sunset matters more to you than an in-depth tasting.

**Best for:** couples, first visits and travellers who want wine as part of a broader Santorini evening.

## Option 3: Go private

Private tours cost more, but they solve a different problem.

They give you control.

Instead of following a fixed winery sequence, you can ask to spend more time on wine and less time on viewpoints you have already seen.

Current private tours on Santorini commonly include hotel pickup and a driver, and some allow optional winery stops such as Santo Wines.

That can be particularly useful if you already know what you want.

For example:

- older Vinsanto
- several expressions of Assyrtiko
- smaller producers
- specific villages
- a slower tasting without a large group

Do not assume every private island tour includes wine tasting in the price.

Check exactly what is included before booking.

**Best for:** serious wine drinkers, small groups and travellers who value flexibility more than price.

## What I would actually look for before booking

Ignore the words “premium”, “authentic” and “exclusive” for a moment.

They appear everywhere.

Instead, check four practical things.

### 1. How many actual wineries are included?

Three proper winery stops are very different from one tasting squeezed into a general sightseeing tour.

### 2. Is transport included?

Do not assume “tour” means hotel pickup.

Some tours use designated meeting points instead.

Read the pickup section carefully.

### 3. Are tastings included in the price?

Some private tours include transportation but charge winery tastings separately.

That is not necessarily bad.

You just want to know before you book.

### 4. Which wineries are named?

A tour that lists its wineries gives you much more information than one promising only a “selection of famous wineries”.

It also lets you check what styles those producers are known for.

## If your real goal is Vinsanto

This is where I would be slightly picky.

Almost every serious Santorini tasting can introduce you to Vinsanto.

But not every tasting gives you the opportunity to compare different ages or styles.

If Vinsanto is the reason you are going, contact the tour operator or winery before booking and ask a simple question:

**Will the tasting include Vinsanto, and which one?**

Even better:

**Is an older Vinsanto available to taste?**

The difference between a younger example and one that has spent many years ageing can be enormous.

You are not just tasting more sweetness.

You are tasting what time does to the wine.

## A note about Santo Wines

Santo Wines is one of the easiest names for visitors to recognise.

It belongs to the Union of Santorini Cooperatives and occupies a dramatic position above the caldera.

For a first visit, it makes sense.

You get the view, a broad introduction to Santorini wine and access to Vinsanto.

It is also popular.

If you are chasing a quiet, intimate cellar experience, this may not be the only winery you want to see.

That is why a multi-winery tour is often more interesting than simply visiting one famous producer.

## A note about Venetsanos

Venetsanos is another winery that appears frequently on organised itineraries.

Its location above the caldera is a major part of the experience.

That makes it particularly attractive for late-afternoon or sunset-oriented tours.

Again, the view is not the wine.

But on Santorini, there is no rule saying you cannot have both.

## My simple recommendation

If wine is only one part of your Santorini trip, choose a small-group tour with three winery stops and included transport.

If the sunset matters just as much as the tasting, choose a wine-and-sunset itinerary.

If wine is one of the main reasons you are visiting the island, go private and tell the guide in advance that you specifically want to focus on Assyrtiko and Vinsanto.

That one sentence can completely change the day.

## Dan’s note

I haven’t personally tried every wine tour on Santorini, so I looked at how the main options actually work — transport, winery stops, tasting format and who each one suits best.

I would not spend a Santorini wine day worrying about who is driving next.

There are too many good wines for that.

Let somebody else handle the road.

Taste the Assyrtiko.

Try the Vinsanto.

Ask annoying questions about old barrels.

And enjoy the fact that for a few hours, logistics are somebody else’s problem.

title: How to Taste Santorini Wine Without Driving
